decisions.quote:
Although some research has found
evidence for these so-called Gettier intuitions, Turri et al. found no evidence that participants attributed knowledge in a
counterfeit-object Gettier-type case differently than in a matched case of JTB. In a large-scale, cross-cultural conceptual
replication of Turri and colleagues’ Experiment 1 (N = 4,724) using a within-participants design and three vignettes across
19 geopolitical regions, we did find evidence for Gettier intuitions; participants were 1.86 times more likely to attribute
knowledge to protagonists in standard cases of JTB than to protagonists in Gettier-type cases.

decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind target 0 identify the same primary target study: Experiment 1 of Turri, Buckwalter, and Blouw (2015, online 2014; DOI: 10.3758/s13423-014-0683-5), 'Knowledge and luck'. The paper is a Registered Replication Report explicitly designed as a large-scale cross-cultural conceptual replication of Turri et al. (2015) Experiment 1.

decisions.quote:
In a large-scale, cross-cultural conceptual
replication of Turri and colleagues’ Experiment 1 (N = 4,724) using a within-participants design and three vignettes across
19 geopolitical regions, we did find evidence for Gettier intuitions; participants were 1.86 times more likely to attribute
knowledge to protagonists in standard cases of JTB than to protagonists in Gettier-type cases. These results suggest that
Gettier intuitions may be detectable across different scenarios and cultural contexts. However, the size of the Gettier
intuition effect did vary by vignette, and the Turri et al. vignette produced the smallest effect, which was similar in size
to that observed in the original study.
decisions.location: Abstract, p. 3, lines 173-179 (see also Results, p. 18, lines 1050-1069; Discussion, p. 26, lines 1509-1551)
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coded the outcome as 'mixed'. The replication tested Turri et al.'s (2015) Experiment 1 findings across knowledge, Gettier, and ignorance conditions. As the authors explicitly state in the Results ('Thus, we did not fully replicate the results of Turri et al., who found no difference in knowledge attribution between the knowledge and Gettier conditions', p. 18) and Discussion (p. 26), they replicated the large difference in knowledge attribution between the Gettier and ignorance conditions, replicated the comparisons against chance for the knowledge and ignorance conditions, replicated the absence of a reasonableness difference between the Gettier and knowledge versions of the original Darrel vignette (p = .064), and found an effect size on the original vignette similar in magnitude to that observed in the original study (OR = 1.86 vs. original OR = 2.00), but failed to replicate the original null difference in knowledge attribution between the Gettier and knowledge conditions. Because the paper explicitly frames its evidence as partly replicating and partly contradicting the tested original findings, 'mixed' is the correct outcome.

decisions.reason: The study collected new empirical data from participants across 37 data-collection sites in 19 geopolitical regions to re-test the published findings of Turri et al. (2015), Experiment 1, making it a replication.

decisions.reason: The paper included luck/ability attribution measures and fit multilevel logistic regression Model 6C specifically to re-test the published moderation finding of Turri (2016, Experiment 7) that attributing true beliefs to luck rather than ability moderates Gettier intuitions (ηp2 = .353), explicitly contrasting its null moderation of the Gettier-vs.-knowledge difference with Turri (2016, 2017). The Reference list confirms the exact identity: Turri, J. (2016), 'Vision, knowledge, and assertion.', Consciousness and Cognition, 41, 41–49, DOI 10.1016/j.concog.2016.01.004. The only shipped row (input_row_index 277, confirmed in prior adjudication) is Turri, Buckwalter, and Blouw (2015, online 2014; 10.3758/s13423-014-0683-5), 'Knowledge and luck' in Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, and sibling target 2 is Turri (2017; 10.1093/analys/anx036) in Analysis; all three are distinct empirical articles reporting separate studies, so report equivalence does not apply.

decisions.reason: In Results ('Luck/(in)ability as a moderator', Model 6C) and Discussion ('Luck attributions'), the authors empirically tested whether attributing a protagonist's true belief to luck vs. ability moderates Gettier intuitions and explicitly compared their finding ('unlike in previous research (Turri, 2016, 2017), luck attributions did not decrease the likelihood of participants demonstrating Gettier intuitions') against the finding attributed to Turri (2017). The Reference list confirms the exact identity: Turri, J. (2017), 'Knowledge attributions in iterated fake barn cases.', Analysis, 77(1), 104–115, DOI 10.1093/analys/anx036. This article is an independent publication distinct from shipped row 277 (Turri, Buckwalter, & Blouw, 2014/2015; 10.3758/s13423-014-0683-5) and from sibling target 1 (Turri, 2016; 10.1016/j.concog.2016.01.004), with no report equivalence.
